hints: Focus on how we make a pure insoluble salt, you need a soluble barium compound first, then precipitate it with sulfate.
Check route 1 first, Ba heated in oxygen gives BaO, which dissolves in dilute HCl to give soluble BaCl2.
Now test routes 2 and 3 for the same pattern, do they both give a soluble barium salt before dilute H2SO4 is added to precipitate BaSO4?
walkthrough:
**Recall the preparation rule**

Barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4$, is insoluble in water. The pure dry solid is best made by precipitation.

You need a soluble barium salt in solution + dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, then filter, wash and dry:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$$

**Check route 1**

Ba metal heated in $\text{O}_2$ gives barium oxide:
$$2\text{Ba} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{BaO}$$
$\text{BaO}$ reacts with dilute HCl to give soluble barium chloride:
$$\text{BaO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Then:
$$\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{HCl}$$
Filtering, washing and drying gives pure $\text{BaSO}_4$. So route 1 works.

**Check route 2**

$\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2$ undergoes thermal decomposition like other Group 2 nitrates to give the oxide:
$$2\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{BaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
$\text{BaO}$ with excess water gives soluble $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$:
$$\text{BaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2$$
Then with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$:
$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
This also gives pure precipitate after filtration. So route 2 works.

**Check route 3**

$\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ neutralised by dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ gives soluble barium nitrate:
$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Then with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$:
$$\text{Ba(NO}_3)_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{HNO}_3$$
Again, filter, wash and dry gives pure $\text{BaSO}_4$. So route 3 works.

**Conclude**

All three routes produce a soluble $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ solution just before sulfate is added, with no other insoluble product to contaminate the $\text{BaSO}_4$. All of 1, 2 and 3 are valid.

options.A: Correct. Routes 1, 2 and 3 all generate a soluble barium salt (BaCl2, Ba(OH)2, Ba(NO3)2) which then precipitates pure BaSO4 on addition of dilute H2SO4. Filtration, washing and drying isolates the pure insoluble salt.
options.B: Incorrect. This option omits route 3. Students sometimes think neutralisation followed by precipitation will leave nitrate contamination, but Ba(NO3)2 is fully soluble and HNO3 stays in solution while only BaSO4 precipitates.
options.C: Incorrect. This option omits route 1. Students sometimes worry that heating Ba in O2 gives a peroxide or that BaO will not dissolve, but BaO reacts readily with dilute HCl to give soluble BaCl2, so the route is clean.
options.D: Incorrect. This option suggests only one route works. A common trap is thinking nitrate decomposition gives Ba(NO2)2 or Ba metal, or that Ba(OH)2 is insoluble, but Group 2 nitrates give the oxide and Ba(OH)2 is sufficiently soluble to use.
